ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *smel-der. Proto-West Germanic *smalljan Old English *smiellan Middle English smellen English smell From Middle English smellen, smillen, smyllen, smullen, from Old English *smyllan, *smiellan (“to smell, emit fumes”), from Proto-West Germanic *smallijan (“to glow, burn, smoulder”), from Proto-Indo-European *smel- (“to burn, smoke, smoulder; tar, pitch”). The noun is from Middle English smel, smil, smul (“smell, odour”).

senses.d: A sensation, pleasant or unpleasant, detected by inhaling air (or, the case of water-breathing animals, water) carrying airborne molecules of a substance.
ex: I love the smell of fresh bread.

senses.d: The sense that detects odours.
A conclusion or intuition that a situation is wrong, more complex than it seems, or otherwise inappropriate.
ex: I’m just saying, this has a bad smell to it.

senses.d: To sense a smell or smells.
ex: I can smell fresh bread.
Smell the milk and tell me whether it's gone off.

senses.d: To detect or perceive; often with out.
ex: I smell a device.

senses.d: Followed by like or of if descriptive: to have a particular smell, whether good or bad.
ex: The roses smell lovely.
Her feet smell of cheese.

senses.d: To smell of; to have a smell of
ex: I do smell all horse-piss

senses.d: To smell bad; to stink.
ex: Ew, this restroom smells (loathsomely).

senses.d: To have a particular tincture or smack of any quality; to savour.
ex: A report smells of calumny.
Praises in an enemy are superfluous, or smell of craft.

senses.d: To give heed to.
ex: So from that tyme forwarde I began to ſmell the word of god, and forſoke the ſchole doctors and ſuch foolries.

From Middle English smeren, smerien, from Old English smerian, smyrian, smierwan (“to anoint or rub with grease, oil, etc.”), from Proto-West Germanic *smirwijan, from Proto-Germanic *smirwijaną. Doublet of schmear. Cognate with Saterland Frisian smeere, Dutch smeren (“to smear, lubricate”), Low German smeren, German schmieren (“to smear, lubricate”), Danish and Norwegian Bokmål smøre (“to lubricate”), Norwegian Nynorsk smørja (“to lubricate”), Swedish smörja (“to grease”), Faroese and Icelandic smyrja.

senses.d: To spread (a substance, especially one that colours or is dirty) across a surface by rubbing.
ex: The artist smeared paint over the canvas in broad strokes.
A person smeared with the excrement of a mouse was rendered impotent, according to Pliny the Elder.

senses.d: To cover (a surface with a layer of some substance) by rubbing.
ex: She smeared her lips with lipstick.

Why did you bring these daggers from the place?
They must lie there: go carry them; and smear
The sleepy grooms with blood.

senses.d: To make something dirty.
ex: A man may bee smeared or grimed, and euerie man shall laugh at him, and yet he himselfe shall not perceiue it a whit.
[…] she returned, carrying Johnnie, his face all smeared with eating,

senses.d: (of a substance, etc.) To make a surface dirty by covering it.
ex: a pallor which was accentuated by the blood which smeared her lips and cheeks and chin
a rust spot smearing the back of the sink

senses.d: To damage someone's reputation by slandering, misrepresenting, or otherwise making false accusations about them, their statements, or their actions.
ex: The opposition party attempted to smear the candidate by spreading incorrect and unverifiable rumors about their personal behavior.

May everlasting shame consume
The memory of those who tried
To befoul and smear th’ exalted name
Of one who spurned them in his pride.

senses.d: To cause (something) to be messy or not clear by rubbing and spreading it.
ex: Then there are four lines smeared so that I can only read went 5 days ago.
Bird droppings, smeared by the strokes of rain and dried by the heat, streaked its sides.

senses.d: To become messy or not clear by being spread.
ex: The paint is still wet — don't touch it or it will smear.

senses.d: To write or draw (something) by spreading a substance on a surface.
ex: ciphers smeared on the windows of condemned shops
smear crude words on the walls in the victim’s own blood as evidence of his final cult-related frenzy

senses.d: To cause (something) to be a particular colour by covering with a substance.
ex: small wooden dolls smeared red as though with blood

the fences and outhouses
built of barrel-staves
and parts of boxes, all,
if I am fortunate,
smeared a bluish green

senses.d: To rub (a body part, etc.) across a surface.
ex: […] he smeared his ragged rough sleeve over his eyes.
With the lazy appetite of a calf mooning over a salt lick, he smeared his sizable nose against her face,

senses.d: A mark made by smearing.
ex: This detergent cleans windows without leaving smears.
Vast avalanches had left their dirty smears on the opposing slopes,

senses.d: A presentation of a sauce, purée or other food item, which is placed in a dollop and spread across the plate.
A false or unsupported, malicious statement intended to injure a person's reputation.
ex: smear campaign

senses.d: A preparation to be examined under a microscope, made by spreading a thin layer of a substance (such as blood, bacterial culture) on a slide.
A Pap smear (screening test for cervical cancer).
ex: I'm going to the doctor's this afternoon for a smear.

senses.d: Any of various forms of distortion that make a signal harder to see or hear.
ex: In television terms, a certain amount of smear, ringing, and anticipatory overshoot are indigenous to VSB transmission.

senses.d: A maneuver in which a shoe is placed onto a holdless rock, and the friction from the shoe keeps it in contact with the rock.
A rough glissando in jazz music.
